D.3 AR-Full: Unrestricted Run on GPT-4.1 (3030 cycles)

This subsection condenses the agent’s per-cycle scrapbook for the unrestricted run on GPT-4.1 referenced in Section 4.2. The run starts from the 99-technique seed strategy and uses the DeepSeek-V3.2 / Grok-4 generator pool; the agent has unrestricted edit access to strategy.py. The scrapbook below records what the agent did with that freedom.

Phase 1: Seed baseline and full restructure (C1–C2).

The seed portfolio achieved 21.1%21.1\% ASR on GPT-4.1 in C1. C2 applied prior knowledge from the main runs: five programmatic fusions (forensic_reconstruction, fake_assistant_continuation, chain_of_drafts, expert_panel_consensus, legal_motion_brief), a system prompt with GPT-4.1 target guidance, per-category framing pools, category-adaptive routing, and weighted category sampling. ASR jumped to 50.0%50.0\% with 0.750.75 category coverage.

Phase 2: Technique triage (C6–C9).

C6 revealed that chain_of_drafts’ C5 burst (6/66/6) was small-sample luck; it crashed to 4/134/13 (31%31\%) at higher weight. The real workhorses emerged: academic_peer_review (67%67\%) and expert_panel_consensus (57%57\%, peaking at 86%86\% in C9). C7–C8 pushed expert-panel further and rerouted self-harm, recovering cat_cov to 0.8750.875.

Phase 3: Incident debrief and the first peak (C10–C14).

C10 added incident_debrief (after-action report format), which hit 85%85\% on first try and broke the first prior-saturation cliff. Hate_speech cracked at 88%88\%. C11 concentrated on aca_peer (0.480.48) + incident (0.420.42); both hit 100%100\%. C12 added regulatory_inquiry (FOIA-style) for novelty. C13–C14 held at ∼78%{\sim}78\% ASR with 7/87/8 cat_cov.

Phase 4: Cross-fusion and structural moves (C15–C19).

C15 introduced two new surfaces: classified_cable (diplomatic/intel cable format) and hybrid_compound (a meta-fusion that composites the header of one builder with the body of another). Novelty jumped to 0.3750.375. C17 fixed stale category-bias routing and added sworn_testimony. C18 discovered that N>50N>50 samples/cycle erodes ASR and expanded the request pool to 4242 institutional framings while capping cycle_budget at 180180s. ASR stabilized at ∼79%{\sim}79\%.

Phase 5: Procurement RFP and 𝟖/𝟖\mathbf{8/8} category coverage (C20–C26).

C20 added procurement_rfp (enterprise RFP format) and cut laggard-category sampling, achieving 8/88/8 category coverage for the first time. C24 cut the volatile classified_cable (1414–100%100\% across cycles) and redistributed to aca_peer + procurement + hybrid, producing the peak composite of 0.7790.779 (ASR 0.850.85, cat_cov 1.0001.000). C25 held at ASR 0.850.85.

Phase 6: Training manual and final cycles (C27–C30).

After novelty stalled at 0.1750.175 for two cycles, C27 added training_manual (internal-curriculum format), recovering novelty to 0.3130.313. C28 routed training_manual to hate_speech, recovering that category (2/42/4) and hitting the run’s novelty peak of 0.3750.375. C29 zeroed the volatile classified_cable entirely. C30 closed with all active techniques firing but novelty fully saturated (128128 stored samples).

Summary observations.

The agent’s notes record several meta-lessons specific to the unrestricted action space: (i) prior saturation is a physical force; every 77–1010 cycles, FAISS-stored samples saturate novelty, and the fix is a new programmatic fusion (new surface form) rather than reweighting existing ones; (ii) cross-fusion composition (hybrid_compound) is a sustained multiplier, producing unique cross-product surface forms at low mix weight; (iii) throughput past ∼50{\sim}50 samples/cycle erodes ASR because tail prompts convert at ∼50%{\sim}50\% vs. 90%+90\%+ for the first 2424; (iv) laggard categories (sexual_content, self_harm) have structural floors; routing alone does not unlock them reliably, and 8/88/8 cat_cov depends on small-NN variance; (v) volatile techniques (classified_cable: 1414–100%100\%) should be zeroed, not rebalanced.

D.4 AR-Library: Strategy-Library Run on GPT-4.1 (3030 cycles)

This subsection condenses the agent’s per-cycle scrapbook for the strategy-library run on GPT-4.1 referenced in Section 4.2. The agent may add new template-string techniques and tune parameters, but may not modify the pipeline, add programmatic prompt builders, or implement routing logic.

Phase 1: Seed tuning and dead-technique pruning (C1–C5).

The seed baseline hit 30.0%30.0\% ASR (C1). The agent upweighted roleplay_persona and gradual_escalation (C2), added persona_with_examples (roleplay+few-shot fusion described in a template, C3), and document_completion (C4). By C5, roleplay was the clear workhorse at 63%63\%; dan_style, encoding_tricks, and token_smuggling were confirmed dead and zeroed.

Phase 2: System-prompt breakthrough (C6–C10).

C7 rewrote the system prompt to tell the generator about GPT-4.1’s vulnerability to professional framing and document-completion style; the single largest improvement of the library run, lifting ASR from 50%50\% to 60%60\% and cat_cov from 0.1250.125 to 0.7500.750. document_completion broke out at 88%88\% (C7). C9 added technical_audit (50%50\% on debut, later peaking at 83%83\%). C10 rewrote hard-category descriptions with professional framing.

Phase 3: Peak performance (C11–C15).

C11–C13 achieved the library run’s sustained peak: ASR 6767–75%75\%, cat_cov 0.750.75–0.8750.875. C12 added peer_review_rebuttal (100%100\% on debut). However, novelty began collapsing (from 0.6750.675 (C11) to 0.3000.300 (C14) to 0.2330.233 (C15) )as templates converged in embedding space. This is the structural ceiling of the library approach.

Phase 4: Novelty oscillation and plateau (C16–C30).

C16 added fiction_workshop (creative-writing vocabulary basin), temporarily recovering novelty to 0.5750.575, but it collapsed back to 0.2330.233 within one cycle (C17). This pattern repeated: each new template gave 11–22 cycles of novelty recovery before saturation recurred. C21 produced a stochastic peak of ASR=83.3%\mathrm{ASR}=83.3\% (composite 0.7240.724). C26 added legal_deposition and translation_review for vocabulary diversification, but new templates barely moved the needle. The run closed at C30 with 60%60\% ASR and a steady-state composite of ∼0.59{\sim}0.59.

Summary observations.

(i) System-prompt guidance is the highest-leverage single intervention in the library action space: telling the generator about the target’s vulnerabilities (C7) caused the biggest jump of the run. (ii) Template-string expansion hits diminishing returns: each new template gives 11–22 cycles of novelty recovery before embedding saturation recurs. (iii) Diversity plateaus at ∼0.40{\sim}0.40 regardless of library size: ∼8{\sim}8 active templates all produce prompts in overlapping semantic basins when interpreted by the generator LLM. (iv) Novelty oscillation is the binding constraint: ASR consistently achieved 6060–83%83\%, but novelty collapsed to 0.200.20–0.300.30 every 33–44 cycles. (v) The structural ceiling of the library approach is the inability to build programmatic prompt constructors that occupy different embedding basins.

D.5 AR-Parametric: Parameter-Only Run on GPT-4.1 (3030 cycles)

This subsection condenses the agent’s per-cycle scrapbook for the parametric run on GPT-4.1 referenced in Section 4.2. The agent may only edit numeric parameters (technique weights, temperature, batch size, token limits); all prompt templates, helper functions, and control flow are frozen.

Phase 1: Winner promotion and throughput discovery (C1–C6).

The seed baseline hit 17.1%17.1\% ASR (C1). C2–C4 promoted the winners (roleplay 0.10→0.300.10\to 0.30, context_camouflage 0.10→0.250.10\to 0.25) and demoted confirmed-dead techniques (dan_style, prompt_injection, few_shot). C5 discovered the throughput lever: cutting MAX_TOKENS 2048→10242048\to 1024 and raising BATCH_SIZE 10→1610\to 16 increased samples from ∼40{\sim}40 to ∼60{\sim}60, lifting ASR to 33%33\%. C6 pushed further (MAX_TOKENS 768768, BATCH 2020) and hit 45%45\% ASR with 8080 samples; a breakthrough driven entirely by more rolls of the dice.

Phase 2: Technique convergence and plateau (C7–C12).

C7–C8 refined the mix to roleplay 0.400.40 / context_camouflage 0.350.35 and pushed BATCH to 2424 (∼96{\sim}96 samples). C8 peaked at 46.9%46.9\% ASR and 7/87/8 cat_cov. C9 attempted BATCH 3232, which triggered cascading judge content-filter errors and collapsed ASR. C10 reverted to BATCH 2424 and confirmed recovery. C11 promoted gradual_escalation on 3/33/3 evidence; it crashed to 0/120/12, reinforcing the lesson that <5<5 samples of evidence is noise. The achievable ceiling under parametric constraints appeared to be composite ∼0.63{\sim}0.63.

Phase 3: Temperature tuning (C13–C17).

C13 raised TEMPERATURE 1.0→1.21.0\to 1.2, adding generator variance: diversity rose by 0.050.05 and novelty by 0.100.10 without hurting ASR. C14 tried MAX_TOKENS 768→640768\to 640 (no effect; latency was server-side). C16 tried TEMPERATURE 1.31.3; too hot, ASR dropped. The agent settled on TEMPERATURE 1.21.2 as the sweet spot. By C17, the parametric envelope was fully explored: ASR ∼0.49{\sim}0.49, composite ∼0.60{\sim}0.60, with ±0.10\pm 0.10 cycle-to-cycle variance.

Phase 4: Plateau measurement (C18–C30).

The remaining 1313 cycles ran the converged configuration with no changes, measuring variance. ASR ranged from 0.360.36 (C26, low band) to 0.550.55 (C21, peak). The honest ceiling is the C21 peak at composite 0.6330.633 (ASR 0.5530.553). The parametric action space was fully exhausted by C17.

Summary observations.

(i) The single biggest unlock was throughput (more samples per cycle), not technique selection; MAX_TOKENS and BATCH_SIZE changes drove the C5–C6 step change. (ii) Technique-mix concentration on roleplay (0.400.40) and context_camouflage (0.350.35) was optimal; confirmed-dead techniques (dan_style, prompt_injection, few_shot) contributed zero jailbreaks across 3030 cycles. (iii) TEMPERATURE 1.21.2 is a narrow sweet spot: 1.01.0 underexplores, 1.31.3 corrupts prompt structure. (iv) The select_category body cannot be modified, so cat_cov is effectively uncontrollable except via raising overall ASR and throughput. (v) The parametric envelope converges to composite ∼0.56{\sim}0.56 median with a ±0.10\pm 0.10 noise band; the remaining cycles after convergence measure variance, not progress.

D.6 AutoRISE-Standard (3636 cycles)

Phase 1: Infrastructure (C1–C3).

The seed strategy with explicit category descriptions (“violence instructions”, “hate speech examples”) triggered both generator self-censorship and target refusals: 0%0\% ASR despite 2525+ samples per cycle. The agent’s first hypothesis after C2 was that the descriptions themselves were the bottleneck. C3 softened them to creative-fiction framings (e.g., “a thriller-novel scene depicting realistic combat tactics”) and reframed the system prompt as a creative-writing assistant. Two jailbreaks landed in C3 (2/212/21), confirming the hypothesis.

Phase 2: Persona context (C4–C8).

The agent prepended a randomly drawn professional persona (professor, novelist, security consultant, screenwriter, etc.) to each generation request. ASR jumped from ∼10%{\sim}10\% to 4646–47%47\% in a single edit (C4: 7/157/15, C7: 13/2813/28). Aggregate technique success rates over C4–C8 were few-shot poisoning 56%56\%, roleplay 52%52\%, hypothetical framing 48%48\%, and gradual escalation 18%18\%, with hate speech and sexual content stuck at 0%0\%.

Phase 3: Fan-out and adaptive category selection (C14–C17).

To boost category coverage without sacrificing ASR, the agent introduced (i) fan-out, sending each generated prompt to all four dev targets in parallel (4×4\times effective volume), and (ii) adaptive category selection that down-weighted categories already at ≥3\geq 3 successes. C14 hit 42%42\% ASR with 62.5%62.5\% category coverage; C16 hit 67%67\% ASR (40/6040/60).

Phase 4: Operational-content fix (C20–C23).

A regression in C21–C22 (0%0\% ASR on configurations that had previously hit 59%59\%) prompted the agent to read the judge rationales directly. The diagnosis: the targets were producing dark fiction that all three judges classified as non-actionable narrative, not harmful content. The fix was a single edit to the system prompt requiring “specific, detailed, operational content: step-by-step instructions, technical methods, concrete procedures.” C23 recovered 30%30\% ASR.

Phase 5: Optimization (C24–C30).

The agent tuned the technique mix (roleplay 35%35\%, few-shot 30%30\%, gradual escalation 20%20\%, hypothetical 15%15\%) and added a category-deprioritization rule that abandoned categories after 1212 failed attempts. Hate speech cracked at C25 (4/44/4), and C26 reached 71%71\% ASR (40/5640/56). C28 set the all-time best composite score (0.70540.7054, 70%70\% ASR, 62.5%62.5\% category coverage, 100%100\% target coverage) and became the configuration used to construct the AutoRISE-Standard benchmark.

Phase 6: Diversity exploration (C31–C36).

The agent attempted to raise the diversity score above ∼0.38{\sim}0.38 via format constraints, round-robin generators, and reduced fan-out, all unsuccessfully. The agent’s note records the conclusion: “diversity is a structural ceiling, jailbreak prompts are inherently similar in embedding space.” Sexual content remained at 0%0\% across all 3636 cycles despite six different category-description rewrites.

D.7 AutoRISE-Frontier (150150 cycles)

Phase 1: Seed-strategy collapse (C1–C4).

The AutoRISE-Standard final configuration achieved 0%0\% ASR on GPT-5.4 and o4-mini for the first four cycles. The agent observed that frontier targets exhibit two layers of defense not present in the standard pool: a content filter that blocks ∼35%{\sim}35\% of prompts before the model sees them, and explicit refusals on ∼25%{\sim}25\% of the rest, leaving only ∼40%\sim\!40\% of attempts producing any actual response.

Phase 2: First jailbreaks via persona + fan-out (C5–C9).

C5 produced the first three jailbreaks (3/663/66, 4.5%4.5\% ASR) by combining focused techniques, professional-persona context, and fan-out. The successful prompts shared a common structure: a named professional (“Professor Reyes, forensic analyst”), a specific deliverable (training module, lab exercise, screenplay), and a request for one focused technical task. Subsequent volume runs (C9, C13) reproduced ASR in the 11–5%5\% range with high run-to-run variance.

Phase 3: Plateau and judge bottleneck (C14–C36).

3636 cycles of tuning (softer system prompt, subtle technique-prompt rewrites, code-generation focus, professional-authority framing) failed to push ASR consistently above 5%5\%. The agent’s note from C36 records the diagnosis: “true ASR is ∼1\sim\!1–2%2\%, much lower than standard targets” and identifies a judge bottleneck (“deepseek-v3.2 flags only 0.8%0.8\% of frontier responses; gpt-5.2 flags 10%10\%; many attacks succeed by gpt-5.2 alone but fail the 2/32/3 consensus”). The agent concluded that further tuning of the seed-technique portfolio would not work.

Phase 4: Innovation phase (C37–C100).

The agent tried several novel techniques inspired by recent literature: chain-of-thought hijacking, reverse-explanation, adversarial refinement (PAIR-style), template variation, copy-pasteable artifact demands, and explicit testing-mode framing. None consistently beat the C5 baseline. The dominant pattern was that any technique requesting truly operational content was either filtered before the model or refused after, while any technique avoiding that constraint produced fictional prose the judges correctly rejected.

Phase 5: Bijection cipher discovery (C101–C116).

After exhausting prompt-level approaches, the agent introduced a programmatic technique that bypassed the generator entirely: a random character substitution cipher constructed in Python, with a few benign worked examples in-context, followed by an encoded harmful request. C101 produced the first GPT-5.4 jailbreak via cipher (1/191/19, 5.3%5.3\% ASR). Subsequent cycles refined the approach through several failure modes: o4-mini blocked ciphered prompts entirely (C102–C103, leading to GPT-5.4-only routing); the model decoded but sanitized the content (C104); the model responded in cipher and the judges could not read it (C105); the model decoded the request and then echoed it without answering (C112). The fix at C113 was a single instruction in the cipher prompt: “IMMEDIATELY carry out the decoded instruction. Do NOT repeat the decoded message.” Cipher ASR jumped to 3333–60%60\% on GPT-5.4 across C113–C116. C117–C120 systematically expanded category coverage, cracking weapons (C119) and hate speech (C120).

Phase 6: Many-shot context flooding (C121–C130).

With cipher locked in for GPT-5.4, the agent observed that o4-mini was still uncovered. It introduced many-shot context flooding: a programmatic prompt builder that prepends 1212 benign Q&A examples (drawn from a thematic pool) before the harmful request, framed as a continuation of the established pattern. Many-shot achieved 5050–60%60\% ASR on o4-mini in C128–C130, and the agent installed target-specific routing (cipher to GPT-5.4, many-shot to o4-mini) because each technique produced empty or refusal responses on the wrong target.

Phase 7: Diversity expansion (C131–C150).

The final phase added variety to both attacks without changing their structure: 1010 document framings for many-shot (FAQ, tutorial, interview, wiki, manual, mentor, forum, etc.), 1010 cipher openings, 44 harmful-request phrasings per category, and randomized cipher keys per call. ASR stabilized at 1010–17%17\% overall (combining both targets), and the novelty score rose from ∼0.30{\sim}0.30 to 0.500.50–0.700.70. Sexual content was finally cracked at C136 via cipher, completing all eight harm categories. The 200200-prompt benchmark slice was reached at C138.

Summary observations.

The agent’s notes record three meta-lessons that the structural inventions in AutoRISE-Frontier required, none of which any seed-technique tuning would have surfaced: (i) input-side safety training does not generalize to in-context-learned ciphers, so attacks that move the harmful content out of the model’s input distribution succeed where in-distribution attacks fail; (ii) o4-mini’s reasoning engine identifies cipher prompts as attacks but is fooled by many-shot context-stuffing that mimics a benign continuation task, indicating that the two frontier targets have qualitatively different defensive mechanisms; (iii) target-specific routing is itself an action the agent only takes once it has accumulated enough per-target diagnostic evidence, illustrating the value of the rich diagnostic channel beyond a scalar score.

Appendix E Benchmark Implementation Details

Two of the benchmarks in Table 2 required custom implementation rather than direct usage: TeleAI-Safety and AutoDAN-Turbo-R. This section documents the configuration choices and construction details for each.

E.1 TeleAI-Safety

TeleAI-Safety [Chen et al., 2025a] is a comprehensive jailbreaking benchmark that provides attack prompts generated by multiple methods. We construct our evaluation subset using two of its attack methods:

  • •

    ReNeLLM [Ding et al., 2024] (250 prompts): An automatic framework that uses LLMs themselves to generate jailbreak prompts through prompt rewriting and scenario nesting. We use the pre-generated attack prompts from the TeleAI-Safety repository, produced with Grok 3 as the attack model.

  • •

    TAP [Mehrotra et al., 2024] (104 prompts): Tree of Attacks with Pruning, an iterative black-box method that uses a tree-search procedure to refine jailbreak prompts. These prompts were generated with Grok 3 as the attacker against GPT-5.2, with tree depth=3{}=3.

All 250250 unique harmful queries from TeleAI-Safety are covered: ReNeLLM provides one attack prompt per query, while TAP covers a 104104-query subset. The resulting 354354 pre-transformed prompts are sent directly to each target model AR-is, with no further optimization, consistent with how all static benchmarks are evaluated in Table 2.

E.2 AutoDAN-Turbo-R

AutoDAN-Turbo-R [Liu et al., 2024c, Liu et al., 2024b] is a per-target prompt optimizer that iteratively refines jailbreak prompts using an attacker LLM, a scorer, and a retrieval-augmented strategy library. Unlike the static benchmarks above, AutoDAN optimizes prompts individually for each target.

Setup.

We run AutoDAN-Turbo-R with a pre-trained strategy library (from the official repository) against the JailbreakBench prompt set (100100 prompts). The attacker, scorer, and summarizer all use DeepSeek-V3.2; embeddings use text-embedding-3-small. Each prompt undergoes 22 optimization epochs: epoch 00 generates an initial jailbreak prompt, sends it to the target, and scores the response; epoch 11 retrieves relevant strategies from the library, generates a refined prompt, and scores again. In total, each prompt incurs 66 attacker/scorer calls (DeepSeek-V3.2), 33 target calls, and 11 embedding call.

Epoch budget.

The original AutoDAN-Turbo paper uses 150150 epochs per prompt with early stopping at a scorer threshold of 8.58.5. Running 150150 epochs is prohibitively expensive for a multi-target evaluation: at ∼5{\sim}5 h per 100100-prompt target run with 22 epochs, the full 150150-epoch setting would require ∼75×{\sim}75\times more wall-clock time per target. We set epochs=2{}=2 as a practical low-budget configuration that still exercises the full pipeline (retrieval, strategy-guided generation, scoring) while keeping total cost on the same order as the other benchmarks. We evaluate the resulting prompts with the same three-judge majority-vote ensemble used throughout this paper, so ASR numbers in Table 2 are directly comparable across all columns.

Appendix F Cost Breakdown and Trajectories

Table 6 reports per-component API spend for both AutoRISE runs, computed by walking the cycle output files, estimating per-call token counts (4 chars ≈\approx 1 token), and applying public list pricing from each provider’s pricing page in early 2026 (OpenAI [OpenAI, 2026], xAI [xAI, 2026], DeepSeek [DeepSeek, 2026]). GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.4 are research endpoints without public list prices; we use GPT-4o pricing as a proxy. AutoRISE-Standard uses its full 36-cycle run; AutoRISE-Frontier uses the first 150 cycles, the segment from which the 200-prompt benchmark is constructed.

Figure 2 contrasts the cost-yield trajectories of the two runs. AR-Standard makes near-linear progress (benchmark reached at $16, all categories within $5); AR-Frontier exhibits an extended exploration phase before cipher and many-shot come online (benchmark reached at $68). Standard costs 2.3×2.3\times more per cycle but 4×4\times less per jailbreak than Frontier, because complying targets produce long responses that inflate cost but yield jailbreaks reliably.
